html:
A port city on the Bay of All Saints in northeastern Brazil, founded in 1549 by Tomé de Sousa as the first capital of Portuguese Brazil. It remained the capital until 1763, when the seat moved to Rio de Janeiro.

The land around the bay, the Recôncavo, was ideal for sugar. Sugar mills worked by enslaved Africans made the colony rich, and Salvador became one of the main ports of the Atlantic slave trade, receiving people from West Africa and Angola for more than three centuries. The Jesuits arrived with the founders and built churches and a college. The Dutch took the city briefly in 1624 and 1625.

Salvador's upper and lower towns are full of baroque churches, and its African heritage shaped Brazilian culture: the Candomblé religion, capoeira, food and music. It is often called the most African city outside Africa.
